title: Paul the Apostle
lead: Paul, also called Saul, was a Jew from Tarsus, a Pharisee who persecuted the first followers of Jesus and then, after seeing the risen Jesus near Damascus, became the best-known missionary of the early church. His letters are the oldest writings in the New Testament, and Acts tells much of his story. Few figures in history have been read, and argued over, as much.

sections.b: Paul was born in Tarsus in Cilicia, a Greek city in what is now southern Turkey, and held Roman citizenship from birth (Acts 22:3; 22:28). He calls himself "a Hebrew born of Hebrews," of the tribe of Benjamin, a Pharisee in his keeping of the Law (Philippians 3:5–6). Acts adds that he was brought up in Jerusalem and trained under the famous teacher Gamaliel (Acts 22:3), and that he made tents for a living (Acts 18:3). He had two names: Saul, the Hebrew name of Benjamin's great king, and Paul (Paulos), a Roman name. Acts uses "Saul" until his first mission (Acts 13:9) and "Paul" after; he was not renamed at his conversion.
sections.refs: Acts 21:39; Acts 22:3; Acts 22:28; Acts 13:9; Acts 18:3; Philippians 3:5–6; Romans 11:1; 2 Corinthians 11:22

sections.b: Paul never hid that he had tried to destroy the church (Galatians 1:13; 1 Corinthians 15:9). The turning point came near Damascus, when, as he puts it, God "revealed his Son in me" and Jesus "appeared also to me" (Galatians 1:16; 1 Corinthians 15:8). Acts tells the event three times, each with its own details (Acts 9; 22; 26). Krister Stendahl argued that it should be called a call, like a prophet's, rather than a conversion: Paul did not change religions but received a commission from Israel's God to take the message to the Gentiles. Alan Segal and others reply that Paul did change communities and convictions so deeply that "conversion" fits too. Both sides agree that Paul himself understood it as a commission (Galatians 1:15–16; Acts 26:16–18).
sections.refs: Acts 9:1–19; Acts 22:3–16; Acts 26:9–18; Galatians 1:13–17; 1 Corinthians 9:1; 1 Corinthians 15:8–10; Philippians 3:4–11

sections.b: Dates for Paul are pieced together from his letters, Acts and a few outside fixed points. An inscription at Delphi dates Gallio's year as governor of Achaia to about AD 51–52, which places Paul in Corinth then (Acts 18:12). Working back with Paul's "after three years" and "after fourteen years" (Galatians 1:18; 2:1), most date his call to about AD 31–36. His mission journeys fill the late 40s and 50s; he was arrested in Jerusalem about 57, held at Caesarea for two years, and sent to Rome about 60 (Acts 21–28). Early Christian writers say he was executed in Rome under Nero, probably in the mid-60s (1 Clement 5; Eusebius, Church History 2.25). How exactly Acts and the letters fit together is still debated (John Knox, Rainer Riesner).
sections.refs: Galatians 1:18; Galatians 2:1; Acts 18:12; Acts 24:27; Acts 28:30–31; 2 Corinthians 11:32–33; 2 Timothy 4:6–8

sections.b: Thirteen letters in the New Testament bear Paul's name. Nearly all scholars accept seven as his own: Romans, 1 and 2 Corinthians, Galatians, Philippians, 1 Thessalonians and Philemon, written in the 50s (Philippians and Philemon perhaps later, about 60–62, if they come from his imprisonment in Rome). Many critical scholars think 2 Thessalonians, Colossians and Ephesians, and most think 1 and 2 Timothy and Titus, were written by followers in his name; many other scholars defend all thirteen. Hebrews does not name its author, and few now think it is Paul's. The letters are real letters to real churches, written to answer their problems, which is why they must be read with their first readers in view.
sections.refs: Romans 1:1; 1 Corinthians 1:1; Galatians 1:1; Philippians 1:1; 1 Thessalonians 1:1; Philemon 1; 2 Peter 3:15–16

sections.h: Paul in Acts and in his own letters
sections.b: Acts never mentions that Paul wrote letters, and its Paul sometimes looks different from the Paul of the letters. In Acts he is regularly linked to the Jerusalem apostles (Acts 9:26–28; 15), keeps the Law (Acts 21:20–26) and preaches in synagogues first; in Galatians he insists he received his gospel from no one and saw only Peter and James (Galatians 1:11–24). Philipp Vielhauer argued that Luke did not understand Paul's theology; others (F. F. Bruce, Colin Hemer, Craig Keener) find Acts a reliable if selective portrait by someone who knew him, perhaps a traveling companion (the "we" passages). Most read the letters as the first source for Paul's thought and Acts as a valuable but secondary account of his career.
sections.refs: Acts 9:26–30; Acts 15:1–35; Acts 16:3; Acts 21:20–26; Galatians 1:11–24; Galatians 2:1–14; 1 Corinthians 9:19–23

sections.h: Jewish and Christian readings of Paul
sections.b: For centuries Paul was read, especially in the West after Augustine and Luther, as the man who found peace with God by faith after failing to earn it by works of the Law. In 1977 E. P. Sanders argued that Judaism in Paul's day was not a religion of earning salvation, which led to the New Perspective (James Dunn, N. T. Wright): Paul's quarrel was over the Law as a badge marking off Jews from Gentiles. A newer Paul within Judaism school (Mark Nanos, Paula Fredriksen) holds that Paul remained a Torah-keeping Jew who opposed only making Gentiles into Jews. Jewish scholars have read him in many ways: as the founder of a new religion, as a radical Jewish critic (Daniel Boyarin), or as a Jewish apostle to the nations. Traditional Protestant, Catholic and Orthodox readings all continue alongside these.
sections.refs: Romans 3:21–31; Romans 9–11; Galatians 2:15–21; Galatians 3:28; Philippians 3:4–9; Acts 21:20–26; Acts 23:6
